lesson_title: R4 to Play, R12 to Win — Do the Maths First
hook_text: Two coins. R4 to play, R12 if both land tails. Sounds generous. Let's see who's actually winning.
clip_script: Two coins at the fun-day stall. Four rand to play, twelve rand if both land tails. Sounds generous. Check it. First, what can actually happen? Coin one is heads or tails. For each of those, coin two is heads or tails. So: HH, HT, TH, TT. Four outcomes. And yes — heads-tails and tails-heads are genuinely different, because they are different coins, even if your palm can't tell. That makes two tails one out of four. Twenty-five percent. Now the money. Let a hundred people play. The stall collects a hundred times four — four hundred rand. About twenty-five of them win, at twelve rand each — three hundred rand paid out. The stall keeps a hundred rand of every four hundred staked. Nothing rigged. Nothing hidden. The prize is just too small for the odds. So what would be fair? Four hundred rand shared among twenty-five expected winners is sixteen rand. At R16, nobody wins in the long run. That one sum decodes every raffle and every lottery ticket you will ever be offered.
visual_style: Two spinning coins dropping into a four-square grid of outcomes, one square lighting gold; then two stacks of banknotes racing — R400 in, R300 out — with the R100 gap glowing on the stall's side of the table.
pacing: Playful setup, crisp four-outcome beat, decisive money reveal, calm final rule.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for tree diagrams, two-way tables and the whole 0-to-1 scale.
